utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. I would like to greet all the people present in the courtroom this afternoon, the representatives from the Prosecution, Defence counsel, and the accused. We need to resume the witness testimony today, but before that, the Trial Chamber is going to rule on four decisions. This will be done orally. The first oral decision to be handed down relates to the joint application filed by the Defence to exclude the testimony of Witness B [as interpreted]. This decision concerns the joint oral application of the 12th of October filed by the Defence with a view to excluding the testimony of Witness B. The Defence has invoked the fact that the witness refused to answer some of the questions put by the Defence teams. The Chamber notes that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence does not allow for the exclusion of such a witness. Paragraph of the Rules, paragraph (A)(i) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence can only state that a witness's testimony is excluded when he refuses to answer an answer -- a question despite a question put to him by the Trial Chamber. This is deemed to be contempt of court. In such a case, such a conviction would have been out of proportion with reality of facts stated. Insofar as contrary to what the Defence has ascertained, the witness in general terms has answered the questions that were put to him with a degree of reticence admittedly, but after having been asked -- after having been asked to respond to these questions. The Trial Chamber feels, therefore, that Witness B -- U's testimony cannot excluded from the case file. However, the Trial Chamber will bear in mind the behaviour of the witness during his testimony when it -- the time will come to assess the weight to be given to the testimony of this particular person. The Trial Chamber will also do this in light of the entire case file. The Trial Chamber therefore asks both parties to specify by next Monday the number of the exhibits which will be asked to be tendered. This has not been done yet. Second oral decision to be handed down today. Oral decision concerning to the objections filed jointly by Defence team to add on more names of the witness list of the Prosecution. On the 2nd of October, 2006, the Defence filed a written motion whereby it objected to the testimony of Terry Cameron and Carry Spork as the names were not on the list provided on the 19th of January, 2006 pursuant to Rule 65 ter of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. In support of this, the Defence has alleged that the Prosecutor has surreptitiously included these two names on the chart of the 14th of September, 2006 thereby providing no further explanation and why these people were called to testify. In its response of the 13th of October, 2006, the Prosecutor reminded us by providing this list on the 6th -- 19th of January, 2006, the Prosecutor had stated that it might still call witnesses whose names were not on that list when and if the testimony of this witnesses would be useful to authenticate some of the documents. And that this would be part of the case of the Prosecution case. This is how the Prosecution justified the calling of these two witnesses. According to the case law of the Tribunal, the Prosecution must, as a general rule, stick to the list of witness of the 19th of January, 2006 pursuant to Article 65 ter (E)(ii) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The drawing up of such a list would become senseless if the Prosecution could just change it as it pleased. Bearing this in mind, the Trial Chamber reckons that if the Prosecution intends to call to testify witnesses whose names are not on the witness list, it must file a reasoned motion to this effect. The Chamber therefore does not rule on the testimony of Terry Cameron pursuant to 64 ter of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Trial Chamber is therefore waiting for the Prosecutor to file a motion on this particular issue and thereby has stayed its decision. Third decision, which is an oral decision, relating to the admitting of documents presented through Witness BR. The Trial Chamber will rule on the admission of the documents presented through Witness BR who testified on the 10th of October, 2006. The Trial Chamber has decided to admit the six following pieces of evidence presented by the Prosecution for the foregoing reasons. They are -- have a probative value and are of some relevance. I shall now quote the exhibits in question: P 00608 under seal, P 00673 under seal, P 03234, P 02999, P 09704, P 00679. In addition, the Trial Chamber asks the registrar to put under seal Exhibit numbers -- documents 00640 and 009376 that have already been tendered and admitted. The Trial Chamber acknowledges the fact that the Defence team has not asked to have any documents admitted. This is our last oral decision relating to the admission of the exhibits presented through Witness BT. The trial will rule on the admission of the testimony of Witness BT, who testified on the 12th of October, 2006. The Trial Chamber has decided to admit the seven following pieces of evidence presented by the Prosecution for the reason that they have a certain relevance and probative value. I shall now give the numbers of these documents. P 09714 under seal, P 03289 under seal, as far as pages 32, 38, 85, and 97 are concerned. P 03948 under seal, P 09696 under seal. That said, this document had already been partially admitted. P 08736 under seal, P 03531, P 03325. Lastly, the Chamber would like to specify the fact that Exhibit number 03234 has already been admitted during the testimony of Witness BR. The Trial Chamber acknowledges the fact that the Defence teams have not asked to have any documents tendered into evidence. In addition, other written decisions have been taken and have been filed, and you can contact the Registry for further details. I have been told that Ms. Alaburic has already had nine minutes of her time. She therefore has 51 minutes left. After that, the Defence counsel of Mr. Coric will have 30 minutes, and we shall hear another witness. I would like the Prosecution to think about this witness's testimony. Perhaps the Prosecution could contemplate Rule 92 ter as far as this particular witness is concerned so that we could gain some time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Williams, good afternoon. I will remind you that yesterday we were talking about two orders issued by Milivoj Petkovic of the 6th and 9th of January, 1993, and I will continue my cross-examination based on those orders. Let me remind you of a document, a milinfosum of the British Army of the 11th of January, 1993, which was shown to you under number P 01094. You may take a look at it, although I will not be asking you about any details. It's P 01094. Paragraph five of this document refers to Gornji Vakuf, and what the document notes for that day is that there was firing on the village of Prusac from the Bosnian Serb army positions. That is that the village was a target of artillery fire. There is a comment noted alongside that piece of information, and that is that Prusac is person for the defence of Bugojno. My question is: In the first days of January, 1993, was there any fighting between the Bosnian Serb army on the one side and the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the other?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which particular area of the country?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The area covered by you, the Gornji Vakuf area. I cannot ask you about other areas because I assume you have no direct knowledge of those.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were exchanges of fire that did not appear to be any big, proper manoeuvre attacks going on. It was mainly just exchanges of fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were going to be talking about Gornji Vakuf? How far is Prusac from Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prusac is by Bugojno so it would probably be -- without looking at a map, at an educated guess, I would say at least 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question I have very briefly. From where the Serb artillery was positioned, could the shells have fallen on Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. Yes. If they brought them close enough to the front line they would be able to shell Gornji Vakuf. During the fighting, within Gornji Vakuf itself and around Gornji Vakuf, there is at least one incident that was recorded, although I can't remember the date, where we believe that one artillery attack that landed near to Gornji Vakuf was actually fired by the Serbs to try -- to get the two combatants to fight again, against each other again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could there have been, as far as UNPROFOR is concerned, that any, likelihood that in those milinfosums when you write that it's the HVO that was attacking with the artillery, that it might have been the Serb artillery firing actually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just that one isolated incident, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, I put this question to you because of the next question I wish to put: The orders issued by Milivoj Petkovic, which we discussed yesterday and which are of a general nature, do they refer to the fighting with the Bosnian Serb army in the nature of things?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall from reading the document yesterday, it was a general order to his OP zone commanders. It didn't specify whether it -- it concerned the Bosnian Serbs or the armija, as I recall the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. Thank you very much. I would now like to go back to your statements about the flag incident from early January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, as you know, the Trial Chamber is controlling the proceedings. You've just spent some time discussing this Serb question. What are you getting at and what are you trying to prove?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the order issued by my client, General Petkovic, was represented by the Prosecution within the context of alleged fighting between the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was a document issued by the 9th of January. My question about the fighting with the Serbs was put with the intention of showing that the HVO was at that time dealing with a conflict with the Serbs. Furthermore, that this was a general order and the way this document was interpreted by the OTP is erroneous. The document refers primarily to the fighting with the Serbs, who at that moment was still the only enemies of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can we be a bit more specific which particular document Ms. Alaburic is talking about, because I'm a bit in the dark about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. This is a document of the 9th of January, about raising combat readiness. P 01087. Let me remind you that this document was shown as a kind of intimation of the -- a conflict with the Muslims in the Gornji Vakuf area, so I feel it my duty to point Their Honours to the true context of that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You affirm what the intention was here. Are you testifying for your client? It says in connection with Geneva talks, and I wonder where from you draw the affirmation that this was primarily aimed at the Serbs. The witness did not say so. The witness says it is indistinct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness answered my question in this way, but if we look at how the witness answered the Prosecutor's question and the context in which this order was put by the Prosecutor, you will see that previously it was interpreted as exclusively an order aimed at the conflict in the Gornji Vakuf area. My intention was not to interpret the document here but simply to clarify the context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question, Witness. As far as you're concerned in military terms, was there any need for the HVO to step up its manpower levels because of the Serb problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, Your Honour, no, there was no actual manoeuvre attacking going on. It was just exchanges of fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this context, by your leave, another order has just been handed to me which I had not intended to tender. It was issued by Zeljko Siljeg on the 8th of January, and in the preamble it says: "Today the enemy had 18 casualties at Kupres." This is Serb army. "And there is a high possibilities that the enemy will fire on villages or infiltrate sabotage groups behind our front lines. Accordingly, I order that combat readiness be raised to highest level at all defence lines." This is a document we will be using further in the proceedings. By your leave, I would like to move on to another topic and that is the flag incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, on Monday you told us that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. This document which you are quoting, does it have a number? Can we see it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document I have just read out is not a document I had prepared to tender now, and for this reason it has not been handed to Your Honours. If you wish to check the accuracy of my reading, the document can be placed on the ELMO and together with the interpreters we can establish what its contents are. However, that had not been my intention because I felt that this would be what I have already elicited from the witness would be sufficient to show what the context is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I trust you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just reading out a document which nobody knows what the document is and nobody has a copy of it, and she's just reading it out into the record. I strongly object by the way this is being done.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will photocopy the document during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You should have done, Ms. Alaburic, to support what you are saying. What you should have said is, the order given by General Petkovic on the 19th of January, 1993 does this apply to the Serbs or no and the witness says no and you pull out your document and you say here I'm showing you a document which concerns the Kupres incident, what do you think about it? And then the document -- you show the document to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, I felt it would be quite sufficient to show the Prosecution document to the witness, P 01094, about the attack of the Serb army on the village of Prusac, which is important for the defence of Bugojno. However, I do not object to putting this document on the ELMO and tendering it, but we will be spending a lot of time on that and I had not intended to dwell on this incident so long. This had not been my intention to do this. So let us move on to the flag incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On Monday, you told us that the flag incident, which occurred in early January, was one of the events that helped raise tensions between the Croats and Muslims. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You also told us that during the ceremony of raising the flag, a Muslim policeman fired shots as a protest, and because of his reaction he himself was shot, and that he was shot by a member of the HVO. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Answering a question by the Prosecutor concerning the events of the 6th of January, 1993, when you were asked to go back to them, in connection with the British Army information referring to that event, document P 01068, you replied that the document reflected that incident. I would now like us to look at this document together. It's P 01068. In this document, the third paragraph, it says: "At around 1800 hours on Monday afternoon, the HVO raised a Ustasha flag in the town." So let's talk about Monday. In the calendar for 1993, Mondays in January -- one of the Mondays in January was the 4th. If Their Honours wish to see the calendar for 1993 I have prepared it, but it's generally available information. If in your report of the 6th of January mention an incident that happened on a Monday, this could only have been the 4th of January.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. This is the battalion milinfosum and it is compiled after all the reports from the outlying stations have been brought in, and so if it says at 1500 hours on Monday, then it will be referring to that Monday the 4th or whatever Monday it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. As you told us about an incident of the 4th of January -- of the 6th, not the 4th of January, interpreter's correction, my question is: Were you referring to the same incident that this information refers to?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without reading to what you're referring to, the 6th of January, I would say this one -- this paragraph here that we are reading now took place on the 4th of January. We had -- our only connection to send information upwards to Vitez was by fax, INMARSAT fax, and we relied on generators and things like that, and so sometimes there were a couple of days delays where for technical problems we couldn't actually push the information upwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Williams --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Witness, I'm a little bit surprised here. You've said that you had technical problems. It was difficult to send your messages, and you're telling us that there were problems as far as electricity was concerned. Fine. And there is an event which has been highlighted by the Defence. This event took place on Monday, the 4th of January, the story about the flags. Did you know that there had been a flag problem in Prozor a few months early on which had caused a lot of problems? Did you know that in Prozor there had been a similar incident in October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We knew that there had been problems in the October in the Prozor area, and -- but the specifics of them we didn't know other than the imam was under house arrest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When a major incident occurs, can't you report this to your superior over the telephone? You had a satellite telephone, didn't you? Couldn't you tell them about this and inform them live as one says in your language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we could, Your Honour, but in October 1992 we hadn't actually deployed. It was just our lead elements that were moving through, and we had problems with the satellite systems, and we had problems maintaining power for the satellite systems, and so sometimes there were delays before we could get information up -- up the chain of command. At that very early stage, the October, November time, we, to be brutally frank, were not particularly bothered what the warring factions did to each other so long as it did not close the route.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, we'd be grateful to you if you'd explain to us what the -- what kind of flag the Ustasha flag is that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- as I recall, it is a Croatian-type flag with a Croatian shield in the centre, red and white chequer-board-type shield with a large U on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And was it that kind of flag with the U in the first square that you saw being raised in Gornji Vakuf at -- at that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it personally. It caused a great deal of friction. Our commanding officer in B Company had both of the local commanders in over it to try to diffuse the situation, and it was the claim of the armija that it was a Ustasha flag.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. Then the situation is clear if that was something that the BH army claimed. Now, let's move on a few days and get to the 13th of January, 1993. Do you remember that on that occasion Mr. Siljeg and Mr. Andric, that they came to Gornji Vakuf for negotiations with representatives of the BH army? And we're talking about the 13th of January now, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be specific about the dates, and I cannot be specific about who was together in which talk, in which set of talks, but I do know Colonel Siljeg came to Gornji Vakuf for talks several times, and I do know that Colonel Andric came.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you remember those talks being held before the heavier conflicts broke out in the second half of January?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I remember or recall the events, there were a series of minor events such as the flag event that you mentioned before that just gradually stoked up and stoked up the situation. There was then a deployment by the HVO, but where they secured a perimeter, so to speak. And then there was the ultimatum, and then there was the main attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. We'll come to that. But do you remember the 11th and 12th of January as reflected in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like I said before, I cannot remember the specific dates, but that was the general order of things. You would have to ask me about something specific for that date.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you something more specific, but I was sure that you remembered the negotiations that took place before the more fierce conflicts began. Now, would you look in my sets of documents and also we'll place the document on e-court, P 01115. It is an order by Milivoj Petkovic dated the 13th of January, 1993, and it relates to conflict situations between the Muslims and Croats, incidents that broke out. And in the introduction, as you're able to see now on your screens, it says and I quote "that over the past few days the relations between Croats and Muslims has deteriorated and in order to prevent any conflicts which go to the detriment of both sides, I hereby order, first of all, that all HVO commands must identify the causes of conflicts in their territory. 2. Immediately establish contact with the Muslim side and solve the problems through talks. 3. Prevent any possible attempts by lower commands to solve the problems that arise. 4. Wherever possible, set up joint teams with the Muslim side to solve the past or current conflicts. 5. Make efforts to remove roadblocks and newly established check-points. 6. To propose a meeting of the commands at least once during the day to analyse the situation on the ground and envisage joint measures. 7. Forward regular and interim reports ..." Mr. Williams, were you aware of these attempts made by the Main Staff to contribute to quelling the situation on the territory of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. There were attempts by both sides to diffuse the situation. However, the -- their success varied. Some cease-fires just never came into effect at all and they were just totally ignored. Some lasted a matter of an hour before it was started again, and some lasted substantially longer so we could get some aid convoys through.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was more or less what it was like. Now, I want to ask you this: Did you know about attempts made by the HVO command to communicate directly with the commanders of the BH army and to have them help diffuse the situation? In that context, let's take a look at a document first, which in my set has the number 4D 00340. And may we have it on e-court as well, please. It is a letter from Mr. Arif Pasalic, commander of the 4th Corps, in which he informs the command of the 3rd Corps of Milivoj Petkovic's order that we looked at a moment ago. From this document, we can see that Arif Pasalic had contacted Milivoj Petkovic to have him help diffuse the situation, that Milivoj Petkovic, pursuant to that issued the order we looked at a moment ago, that Milivoj Petkovic informed Arif Pasalic thereof, and that Arif Pasalic in his turn then informed the command of the 3rd Corps. Did you know that the commanders of the two armies at the level of command -- the commands endeavoured to solve the problems on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They gave the impression that they were trying to solve the problems on the ground, yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Now, with respect to the alleged ultimatum that you mention, I'd like us to look at a document first P 01174.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please, before we go on to the next document. I'd like to go back to the other document, 00340. Witness, could you take a look at (c), 2(c), paragraph 2(c).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you read the sentence out to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says, Your Honour, possible attempts by lower commands to try to solve arisen problems by force are to be stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, in your opinion, how would lower commands be -- how would it be possible for lower commands not to follow the orders issued by superior commands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this particular time, you would have to appreciate that there were an awful lot of people with guns, and so the commanders would meet with some success in getting their proper troops under control, but renegade elements would not stop, and that would slowly suck the regular troops back in to -- to fighting, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And you, Mr. Williams, for that clarification. Now, the next document that I'd like us to take a look at is P 01174, and it is a document signed by the commander of the 3rd Corps of the BH army, Enver Hadzihasanovic, and it refers to talks held on the 16th of January, 1993, which you described to us during your testimony and which are referred to in the BritBat document for the 16th of January. Let's start off by seeing what Hadzihasanovic wrote, and then we'll compare this with the BritBat document. Hadzihasanovic, and that's at the end of the second sentence, said that at a meeting the representatives of the HVO presented the express -- their express views with the demands they wanted to be carried out. Set forth an explicit position with the demands they wanted to be carried out. Now, at the end of the document, it says: "Regardless of their interpretation, these demands were not an ultimatum." Now, on the basis of those two sentences, would it be valid to conclude that the representatives of the HVO once again emphasised that it was not an ultimatum but that they were explicit demands?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was delivered as an ultimatum with a 24-hour deadline, and I think if you look at page 2 it mentions that, where it says if these demands are not carried out by tomorrow at midnight or there is no desire to carry them out, they will not wait for the following day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, whether it was an ultimatum or explicit demand, I suggest we deal with that issue later on, but tell me now whether the representatives of the Croats at that time meeting, according to what Hadzihasanovic recorded, did they say that it was an explicit demand?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They read out a list of what they wanted and gave the armija 24 hours to comply.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, if we look at what the representatives of the HVO demanded of the BH army, and we can look at that together, the bullet points or sentences after the bullet points, we don't have a lot of time to go through it all, but if we could look through it quickly. To pull out the units towards the villages, to have all units returned to the places they came from in the first place, which refers to Jajce. And I'm skipping over a few sentences now. To establish a joint check-point with proportionate representatives of the Croat and Muslim side, and it is necessary to have a mixed composition of military policemen, and all militant units to be withdrawn to the villages and town. Gornji Vakuf must not have a single soldier with a long weapon with the exception of a mixed military police patrol. Now, we can skip over the other parts. I think that will suffice. It's enough for my question. Now, these proposals, did they go along the lines of demilitarising Gornji Vakuf in a sense, and would not compliance with those demands in fact have meant that in Gornji Vakuf no conflicts could break out by the same token?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If those demands had been put in place and had been applicable to both sides, the HVO and the armija, then, yes, probably there would have been no conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was true for the BH army and not for the HVO? Because it says all militant units. So which -- that does not mean just the BH army. It would apply to the HVO as well.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. As I -- as I just replied, if it -- if it would have been applied to both sides, then, yes, it would probably have stopped the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to tell you that it did apply to both sides. That's what I wanted to say. It was a proposal that applied to both sides.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree it was a proposal that applied to both sides, but it never came into effect on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And tell me, please, could it have taken root if the Bosnian Herzegovinian army never accepted it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because if -- if the armija wouldn't accept it, then neither would the HVO. So basically it was a blanket thing. They either both complied with it or neither of them would comply with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Do you agree that the situation was as follows: That the HVO made this proposal, which was to have applied to both sides, whereas the BH army did not accept that proposal, and because of that, the proposal couldn't be put into effect, take root?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like us to compare this report by Enver Hadzihasanovic with the BritBat report. The number is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. This document is important, and I'd like some -- something to be specified. The negotiating commission to resolve the problems in Gornji Vakuf, the conflict there was made up of HVO representatives and BHA representatives, and we can see Colonel Merdan among them. This report was also signed by the commander of the 3rd Corps. It appears that this report is the subject of a discussions between the BH army and the HVO, and it would appear that the HVO explicitly stated its point of view in formal terms. And I'm reading the first sentence where it says that the organisation of provinces is based on reciprocity. And the second sentence says that there was -- that they were in touch with Geneva because this could be modified in Geneva. Now, one gains the impression that -- and drawing conclusions from that that the HVO is demanding of the ABiH to withdraw its units, et cetera, and to subordinate the ABiH to the HVO with an HVO commander. And then I can see that they don't want the BH army to be commanded with Topcic, Agic, and Prijic, and that the new commander -- designated commander would be Commander Merdan, Colonel Merdan. Now, on page 2 of that same document, General Hadzihasanovic indicates that this does not represent an ultimatum but a categoric position, and that he considers that the demand is in fact an ultimatum. Now, what do you think about all that? The demands made by the HVO formulated through this commission, did they reflect the atmosphere of the times, because it was a meeting that took place on the 16th of January, 1993? So the HVO taking these positions, does that correspond to what they were thinking at the time? And perhaps you described that situation through your milinfosums, or did the local HVO commanders tell you about that? Was that their position you would say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The -- the -- the bullet points in the document are -- are the points that were brought up as part of what I refer to as the ultimatum. The reason we called it an ultimatum was because of the time zone on it, that they had to be done within 24 hours, or else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as far as you were concerned, you had the feeling that the HVO was in fact putting an ultimatum to the BH army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, because of the time limit on it. And the threat, Your Honour, that they would take further action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If one would -- would formulate very succinctly, is the demand not almost a demand to surrender?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, Your Honour. The -- from the Muslim perspective, yes, they regarded it as a surrender, and they were not prepared to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I note, Witness, that at the end of the document, and you can take a look, the last paragraph, the 3rd Corps commander demands that Izetbegovic is informed of this demand -- these demands. What is your interpretation of that? Was the situation that serious that President Izetbegovic, who was the Supreme Commander of the BH army, should be informed? Did it merit that? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I recall the events of the time at a higher level, the -- this particular incident would, if it went ahead, derail the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, and that was why probably Colonel Merdan wanted his president to be aware of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, I'm now going to show you another document that we've already discussed and which I consider to be the key document furnishing your opinion that this was indeed an ultimatum. Take a look at the Prosecution's set of documents, their bundle, and it is document P 01163. I did not prepare this document for Their Honours because I assume that Their Honours still have the Prosecution bundle for this witness. It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rest assured, Counsel, that we do have it. Yes. It's not leaving the table.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It is a report by BritBat for the 16th of January, and under point E, the meeting is recounted, and the alleged words used by Colonel Andric or recorded, and the one but last sentence or two penultimate sentences of Andric's alleged words in the BritBat report read as follows and I quote: "There are two HVO brigades in Prozor, supported by tanks and artillery which are ready to advance towards Gornji Vakuf. You have until tomorrow to meet all our demands and to act upon them or to confront the consequences as an alternative." If you have had time to look through Enver Hadzihasanovic's report in its entirety does he mention 2 brigades in Prozor ready with tanks and artillery to move towards Gornji Vakuf, or did he hear something like -- or did the BritBat representative just hear of things like that that recorded the minutes of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What the notes here in the -- or the entry here in the milinfosum is virtually word-for-word a translation of what was written down in that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I conclude that you cannot comment on how the BritBat member who wrote this or attended the meeting heard about the brigade in Prozor, the artillery and tanks, how they came to hear of it, whereas Enver Hadzihasanovic didn't. You can't comment on that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment on that because I do not know what General Hadzihasanovic did or didn't at this particular moment in time deem the most important piece of information to get to his president.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Fine. Now we can move on to the events -- or, rather, the documents after the conflict, the 19th of January, and all those documents so that we can see the efforts made by the top-ranking HVO commanders to calm the situation down in -- on the ground. When you spoke about the chain of command in the HVO, the hierarchy there, you said that Zeljko Siljeg -- that Milivoj Petkovic was Zeljko Siljeg's superior your in Mostar. Do you know who was another of Zeljko Siljeg's superiors? Do you know who the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of Herceg-Bosna was, for instance?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't -- can't recall, because I never actually met or dealt with any paperwork concerning those gentlemen. I Just know Milivoj Petkovic was, as I believe, the Chief of Staff for the HVO up at Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us now take a look in my bundle at a document numbered P 01211. It is an order by Mr. Mate Boban, who was the Supreme Commander of the armed forces. I see that you're nodding. Does that mean that you've just recollected that it was Mate Boban who was the Supreme Commander? Have you just remembered that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I misinterpreted your question. When you were referring to earlier on, I thought you meant military-wise. Mate Boban was like a politician-type person.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mate Boban was a politician, yes, but a civilian in all countries is head of the army, in all democratic countries, and that what it was in BH. He was the supreme -- on the 19th of January, Mate Boban issued an order on banning HVO forces from implementing any offensives vis-a-vis the BH army. I don't want to read the whole document now, but tell me, the document was sent to the representative of the defence department or, rather, the head of the defence department and the Chief of Staff. Did you know that the number one man of the armed forces of Herceg-Bosna, on the 19th of January, issued an order ordering a stop to all combat operations?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably would have known at the time, but I don't recall it now because there were that many orders going down all the time to tell them to stop fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's look at what happened on the following day. P 01238 is the document. The 20th of January. It's a joint order issued by Milivoj Petkovic and Arif Pasalic, concerning the cessation of all combat activities on the entire territory of Gornji Vakuf municipality, between the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Tell us, were you aware that Milivoj Petkovic and Arif Pasalic issued such an order jointly?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I would have probably known at the time, but I cannot recall specifically now. Like I said before, that were that many orders coming from commanders to tell them to stop fighting, sometimes two or three a day, that -- specific ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did these orders arrive in your headquarters, the headquarters of your command? As a rule, did you know about the existence of documents such as joint orders issued by the highest-ranking officers?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, yes, we as UNPROFOR in Gornji Vakuf were made aware of these orders. And then they were passed down to our soldiers as well that a cease-fire was about to come into effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now look at P 01293. This is a handwritten document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. The Defence counsel has just shown you an order dated the 20th of January, which is specific insofar as it's signed by both authorities, Petkovic and Pasalic. When you read the order, you can see that this order makes UNPROFOR play a role. It specifies that UNPROFOR, as well as the ECMM, must organise a meeting between the commanders of the HVO BiH and ABiH. You seem to be saying that you don't recollect this order. Are you quite sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, yeah. The specific order itself is just one of order after order after order about cease-fires. There were cease-fires where the UNPROFOR and the ECMM were involved, but I cannot be specific to specific orders and specific dates. I just do not remember the actual intimate detail of which date which order was given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Evidently there were some combat activities even after this order was issued, and for this reason on the 20th of April, in document P 01923, Milivoj Petkovic issued another order. This order was issued from Geneva on the 24th of January, and the document before us is not dated. However, from a subsequent document issued by Zeljko Siljeg, which refers to this order, we will see that it is an order issued on the 24th of January. Milivoj Petkovic was in Geneva, and there was he informed that the conflicts had not ended. Therefore, he issued this order from Geneva that the HVO units in Gornji Vakuf should cease offensive actions against the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And he also insists that Mate Boban's order of the 19th of January, which we saw today, be complied with, as well as the order of the 20th of January that we have seen here today. Tell us, were you informed about the attempts of the most senior people in the HVO staff to have these conflicts stop?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were aware that at senior level they were trying to stop it. However, their ability to control their own troops was letting them down all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Evidently, even after this order the fighting did not stop completely. So let us look at document 4D 00358.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Let's still talk about this written order which comes from Geneva. Could you look at this, please. This order, strangely enough we see the order "Urgent" mentioned three times. Normally speaking, you write the word "urgent" once only. Quite clearly, the person who wrote this order put the word in "urgent" three times. As I can see that this must have been sent by mail -- by e-mail. This is Colonel Siljeg's e-mail address here. At item 1, we can see that the HVO unit at Gornji Vakuf must cease operations against the ABiH straight away, and the units must obey Mate Boban. How do you understand this? According to you, the HVO units had not complied with the cease-fire and were still attacking the ABiH. Can you give us an explanation for this, or is the order based on wrong data?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, Your Honour. As it says in the order that HVO units in Gornji Vakuf are to cease offensive operations immediately. Yes, there were still attacks going on all the time. In the end, our commanding officer Colonel Stewart stopped using the word "cease-fire" and started used the word "a reduction in firing" instead because he thought that cease-fire was just a word that was meaningless in that situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say Colonel Siljeg was not complying with the orders, because of his own accord --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. From reading this I would say that Colonel Siljeg was having problems with some of his sub-units and was trying to make them comply with the order and that they weren't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So why did the sub-units go on fighting? What kind of explanation can you provide for this given that the negotiations were under way in Geneva and General Petkovic was in Geneva in person, and the representatives of the ABiH were also in Geneva? How can you explain this? As negotiations were under way, a cease-fire had been decreed as was stated in the previous document we just saw which was signed by Mate Boban. How could the units still be fighting? You were an observer in charge of intelligence. How can you -- do you understand this discrepancy about what's been decided in Geneva at the highest levels of the HVO and that units on the ground were still fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The main problem was that the soldiers were not under control enough, and as a result, a minor -- we would get a cease or a stabilisation of the situation and a reduction of fire, and then a minor incident between two villages or even just two other soldiers somewhere else would slowly suck them all back in again. For instance, there were two particular villages above Gornji Vakuf who seemed to be having their own little war between themselves. And so although you could get the troops from both sides to stop, this village would continue fighting and it would slowly suck the troops back in. And that was why the cease-fires used to keep collapsing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of any action being taken thereafter to discipline the commanders who had obviously disobeyed orders, or was this simply passed under silence, or were there any efforts to improve the enforcement of orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am personally not aware of any discipline taken against commanders who disobeyed their orders. However, these breaches were brought up in negotiations and both sides said that they would deal with the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With my colleague's indulgence. When he says "sucked in" I think that needs clarification, because if I understand the witness correctly, he's saying these undisciplined soldiers were provoking and the provocations would cause clashes. I think that needs some clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Basically to put it simply, the example I used was the two villages. They would not stop fighting. One village was Croat, one was Muslim. The soldiers nearby then got edgy about whether their particular ethnic village was going to be attacked properly or not, and so they would start firing in support of their village, which would then mean that the other side's soldiers would start firing in support of their village, and it would slowly stack up again and the cease-fire would then collapse, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, based on what you have just told us, to the best of your knowledge and based on your experience as a professional soldier, please tell us, could it be said that the HVO commanders had effective control over the units on the ground, or, rather, over all the men who were carrying weapons and participating in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: By and large the commanders on both sides managed to control their men. However, there were renegade elements who were out of control, who destabilised the situation again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But that would mean that they did not have effective control over combat activities in a certain area. Would that be correct? If something happened that they were unable to control, this would mean that they did not have effective control over all the events in a certain area. Would that be a logical conclusion from everything you have told us?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would. They -- they would try to exert control, but some of the soldiers were reluctant to stop fighting and so just carried on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's imagine that such a situation would have occurred inside a British Battalion. For instance, a British Battalion would not comply with the orders. What would have happened? What would the commander have done in such a situation, and what must a commander do in such a situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The immediate commander of the sub-unit or even the individual concerned would be removed from his position there and then on the spot, as would the soldier himself or sub-unit itself, and they would then face disciplinary action, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given your fair knowledge and understanding on the ground, during this period of time, had you knowledge of disciplinary action being taken against the culprits.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had no knowledge, Your Honour, of any disciplinary action being taken. I cannot say whether it was or was not done.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, when you told us what would be done in similar situations were soldiers or officers of the British Army involved, let me ask you the following: How long did the British Army need to establish rules, a hierarchy, and discipline enabling a military soldier or an officer to be immediately punished?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The history of the British Army is long and convoluted. We had a regular army that we have now from about the mid-1960s onwards when we did away with conscription. It has a set of regulations called the Queen's regulations, and they are adhered to and soldiers dealt with accordingly. There are -- we have what we call SOP, Standard Operating Procedures, and we have standing orders, which is how they would behave at all times. And the discipline within the British Army, if you breach it, is quite severe to the extent that -- and you are held responsible for your men all the time. And I can give you an example of that where I was find 300 pounds because one of my soldiers had some ammunition and I was in hospital having an operation at the time. That is the level of discipline within the British Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. I just wanted to hear that one does need a long tradition and it takes time for things to begin functioning properly. But to go back to my question which was about effective control. So to conclude, there were groups that could not be controlled. We said that the commanders could not have effective control. And my last question would be: It follows from everything you have said that those commanders, with respect to those individual groups, could neither command nor control their activities. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In specific areas, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just need to know how much time I have left in order to make the best use of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please. You've had 44 minutes. You had 51 minutes left. You therefore have seven minutes left. So if you could finish in seven minutes time and then we'll have the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, please take a look at document P 01344 in my set of documents. So we have now finished with Milivoj Petkovic's order of the 24th of January from Geneva. On the 25th, all fighting stopped. And now another document was issued on the 29th of January addressed to Zeljko Siljeg, who was at that time in Prozor, where the chief of the main HVO staff demands first that "All our extremists be arrested and locked up." It's P 01344. You can see it on the monitor as well. "Arrest and imprison all our extremists. 2. Give a sharp warning to people from the command who resist you and think differently. 3. Point out to the other side that you have given instructions for a list to be made of Muslim refugees from Gornji Vakuf municipality in the Republic of Croatia and that we will return them to Vakuf as soon as possible. This is my order. And really do charge someone from the civilian structure with obtaining a list. We will sort out Bugojno as soon as possible," and so on. If you wish to comment the remaining points, that's fine, but these are the most important ones for us. Did you know that the highest-ranking HVO officers were trying, through their orders and activities, to establish order to the maximum extent possible under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment in time they were giving us assurance that they were trying to get renegade elements under control, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I add a question. Did you also see an echo of this order? Was there any change in the behaviour? Did you -- did you observe an effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, yes. There was -- there was a change in position of the HVO from -- during late January where they became more interested in defusing the situation and getting some sort of effective cease-fire into position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, could we just clarify your responses to His Honour Judge Antonetti's questions as to whether HVO soldiers spent nights at home or in barracks. From your response, one could conclude that those who were married slept at home and that those who were not married slept in barracks. That is why I will put the following series of questions to you: In the factory where the HVO Brigade was quartered or where it had its seat, that was in the immediate vicinity of the BritBat headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was next door to us. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In this factory, were there any dormitories there or no? Is it correct to say that there were no dormitories there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment either way. I never went into the factory itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, was there anything else there apart from the command of the Ante Starcevic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best -- again, to the best of my knowledge they had some sort of stores or supplies there, and you would see lorries or small trucks coming and going, delivering things and picking things up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I conclude from your report that nothing happened on the basis of which you might conclude there were dormitories there and that soldiers slept there. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot -- again, I cannot comment either way. Where they slept was by and large up to them. It -- we noted some buildings that were used as billets for troops, but it was not a big concern of ours where they slept.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, was it a rule for military units to be active in a certain area composed of local people, people who actually lived in the area?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- both the local armija brigade and the local HVO Brigade were mainly local, and within the armija organisation, there was the TO who were mainly village defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You told us about shifts going into combat, so let me ask you the following: If soldiers were not holding the shift on the front lines, they could be in their own homes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We worked on the assumption from what we had seen that they had a shift that involved a period of time on the front line, a period of time doing administration and sorting things like that out, a period of time getting ready to go back to the front line and then a period of time back on the front line. So we worked on the assumption that it was probably roughly one-third in each bit as they -- as they rotated round.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In other words, whether a soldier was married or not was not a precondition for their spending nights at home. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would -- the welfare of the HVO I know little about, but I would assume if they operate along the lines of other armies they would allow married soldiers to go home, and they would allow soldiers who lived locally, whose parents or whoever lived there, to go home for a period of leave, R and R.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, General Praljak would like to intervene, so I will cede to him my right to put the next question. The question is exclusively to do with shifts and the marital status of soldiers, so it's of a technical nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Does he want to deposit as a witness or as an expert, or is there any other way in which we can hear him in this context? I think not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, Judge Trechsel, Mr. President. It is -- it is well-founded in this Tribunal that normally Defence counsel and Prosecution are allowed to ask questions following questions posed by the Judges. I assume that General Praljak wishes to add a question based on questions posed by the Judges as I have two particular questions that I would like to ask for clarification purposes. I think it is a well-founded rule, because generally, not always but generally, Judges reserve questioning until after the parties have questioned. I'm not saying that that's -- that should be the practice, but there may be times, and this may be one of them, where one or two questions may be sufficient. So it's not out of practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Alaburic, so it will be taken away from your time. Mr. Praljak, put your question to the witness now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A very simple question. The barracks that the witness mentions was very near the BritBat in Vakuf. The question is as follows: Did you ever see soldiers exercising or having breakfast in the compound where the supposed barracks would have been? Because soldiers come out, and they exercise or relax or have breakfast or something like that. So was it just a gathering point for people before leaving for the ground, or was it a barracks in that sense that they slept there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the question. Like I said, I never went inside the building, so I can't say what went on inside it. We used to see soldiers coming and going all the time and vehicles coming and going all the time. We viewed it as the headquarters of the local brigade. Whether the soldiers actually lived in there properly, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may General Petkovic ask a question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one question to this witness. Witness, you keep referring to Territorial Defence unit here. Do you know when the Territorial Defence units were abolished and no longer existed in the BH army but the army of BH was formed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your question, General. The date of the formation of the BH army I do not know at all. The BH army themselves used to refer to these units as TO, which is how I even know it's pronounced TO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, during that time you were there, the BH army couldn't have told you that it was the TO units, because as such, they did not exist. They were abolished and the BH army established. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The local army commanders used to refer to these units as TO, General. We only have what the local army commanders tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My time is up. Thank you for the time allotted us. Thank you, Mr. Williams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's quarter to 4.00. We're going to take a break for 20 minutes and reconvene at five past 4.00, at which time the next Defence counsel, Mr. Coric's Defence counsel, will have 30 minutes for their cross-examination, and then we'll conclude because there's a second witness waiting. We reconvene at five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's addendum: In the first oral decision handed down today by the Presiding Judge, the Rule referred to is Rule 77, contempt of the Tribunal. I quote the Tribunal in the exercise of its inherent power may hold in contempt those who knowingly and wilfully interfere with its administration of justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll try and be as brief as possible, and if any technical explanations are needed, then my client will ask the questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Dijana Tomasegovic Tomic. I'm an attorney at law from Zagreb, and I will be cross-examining you on behalf of the fifth accused in this case. Would you take the Prosecution bundle that you have before you and look at P 01250. For e-court, it is page 3 of the document, paragraph 5. The title is "Gornji Vakuf" in the English version. In the Croatian version, it is also page 3, paragraph 1 this time. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: It's dated the 21st of January. It is from your regiment. Is that right? A milinfosum?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I'll start reading the passage that I mentioned starting out from line eight of the English version in which it says as follows: "It was reported that HVO forces this morning destroyed the majority Muslim populated village of Hrasnica, TT 0441. The HVO soldiers responsible were believed to be wearing blue helmets and to be equipped with three BTR-40s, armoured vehicles. A blue BRDM-2 was reported to be located on the main road junction GR 0272. Comment. Gornji Vakuf believe that these soldiers may have been from a Herzegovinian military police unit." While I was reading, I tried to emphasise "alleged" and "possible." Now I'm interested in the following: Am I right in concluding, in view of the words I emphasised, that the individual who compiled this report was not quite sure about the reliability of this piece of information?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not quite correct. The -- the person who compiled the report was actually me. It was from debriefing a patrol on the ground, and unless something as specific as this, unless I personally had seen it, I would have to use a caveat, the caveat being "believed." I can't say that that is what he saw. I can only say that that is what he told me he saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And that somebody who told you he saw it couldn't tell you which unit they belonged to, but they could possibly belong to a military police unit. I assume you knew which unit of the military police and from what -- or, rather, had you known which unit and from what town then that person -- or, rather, you would have written that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me now, please, yesterday in response to questions from Mr. Murphy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just a moment. I'm looking at the rest of that passage. You said that it was you yourself who wrote that report. Now, I'd like to know whether you also wrote that "the BiH claimed to be holding 20 Croatian prisoners of which they allege 17 were from a Croatian HV special forces unit which was normally based in Split." So did you write that mention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when you say the BiH told you, who told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- the BiH officers that were in our base. It was one of the points they brought up during one of the cease-fire negotiations when -- as a gesture of goodwill, our commander used to try to get them to divulge on both sides how many prisoners they had, et cetera, et cetera, and try to get them to swap them back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And were they actually exchanged, those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, I'm sure you'll remember, yesterday in response to questions from my learned friend Mr. Murphy, you said that the members of the army that you say were military police with the blue helmets and blue armoured vehicle, that you saw them only once from a distance of 150 to 200 yards. That's what you said yesterday, is it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, that was my personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now, do you remember when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be specific on a date, no, I'm afraid not.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, I assume in view of the distance from which you saw them that you weren't able to talk to them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to remind you of your first day in the courtroom, and during the examination-in-chief I think that this question was posed by His Honour Judge Antonetti with respect to the identification of individual units, HVO units, why in your reports it doesn't say exactly what units these HVO members belonged to. And you said at the time that you couldn't do that every time because the only way you were able to identify them, which unit, which HVO soldier belonged to, was if you talked to him and then that he told you that. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you look at the Prosecution bundle again, the next document, P 03090. In the English version it is on page 26, and in the Croatian it is page 22. May we have it on e-court, please. It is a report on the work of the military police of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, an analysis of the situation from between January to June, 1993. You remember the document I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you just confirm its 3090 and what page, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we'll have to have that repeated because there was no English interpretation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat. The document is P 03090. In the English version, it is on page 26, the last two paragraphs, and the first paragraph of 27. For the Croatian, it is page 22, last paragraph on that page, and page 23, first paragraph. We have it on our screens, both pages. From what you're looking at, I assume you can say that this part of the report relates to the logistics service 233. And then the "Quartermaster Service" is the last heading. And I think you'll agree that it is a service which deals with logistical matters, supplies to soldiers.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you to look at part of the text under the title of "Quartermaster Service," which begins the following words, for example -- it says: "For example, in this period we were issued with and distributed: 1 camouflage trousers," so many pieces. I don't have to read the figures. "Camouflage jackets," once again the quantity. "Camouflage shirts, white belts", and under 5, "VP military police badges or flashes". Now, among this equipment, do you see helmets mentioned at all? I think it is obvious that there are no helmets mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see there are no helmets mentioned and no boots either.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now, would it be logical that those helmets would have to have been on the list if they had been issued to the soldiers during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was part of this issue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on e-court I'd like a Prosecution document which isn't in the bundle to be put on the monitor, on the screen. 00956 is the number. And may we look at the first page. While we're waiting for the document, it is the same type of document as the previous one, but the period is different. It is from April to December, 1992. Comprises that period. There's the first page. It is a military police report one again. Now, on e-court, page 15 of the English and page 14 of the Croatian, please. On the English page it says "Logistics" again. May we turn to the next page, that is to say, page 16 in the English. And we see a table there with the following: It says the type of military police unit on one side, and at the top it says "Type of equipment." Then we have "Handcuffs," so many pieces. In the Croatian version this is page 15. So the next page, please, for the Croatian. It says page 14 in the Croatian. Not that table. That's the wrong one. Page 14, please. That's 13. Next page, please. But the English version is the proper page. It says "Handcuffs," so many pieces, "White belt," so many, "Stop sign," and then the figure, "Badges," and the figure, "Coat of arms," and the figure, and "Insignia," also the number there. There are no helmets either. So I assume that your answer would be the same as it was last time, that had they been issued during that period of time, they would have been included in the table; is that right? Is that what you'd said?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that. And again, I point out it doesn't mention boots either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, would you agree that also no clothing, no trousers, et cetera, were distributed in that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to that table that I'm looking at, Your Honour, yes, I would agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Would you take up document P 3090 or 03090 once again. The document we saw a moment ago. The English version is page 6 and 7. Last paragraph on page 6 and first paragraph on page 7. And in the Croatian version page 5, last paragraph, and the first paragraph of page 6. It is the same report. I'm going to start reading. Have you found the page?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: It says: "Operative zone of North-west Herzegovina." It's been read already but not in its entirety. "At about 0800 hours on the same day, the Military Police 2nd Battalion members from Livno and Posusje, consisting of 30 military policemen, took control of the village of Uzricje by which the ABiH circle around the town was penetrated. At 1435 hours, the military police 1st Light Assault Battalion members took control of the village of Zdrince, which was already under BiH control." And then on the next page: "During that time, the members from the 2nd Battalion from Prozor took a number of villages and important features held by the BH army in the part of the municipality which borders with the municipalities of Prozor and Konjic." In this report we can see that mention is made of two particular villages, and they are Uzricje and Zdrince, and apart from that, other villages are mentioned in part of the municipality bordering on the municipalities of Prozor and Konjic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: We cannot see any mention of the village of Hrasnica there at all; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now on e-court may we have the next document T 09276. It is a collection of maps. Map 16, in fact. The ERN number is 05045969. That's the map we need. It shows the Gornji Vakuf area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just -- I'm looking at the witness, and he's looking at the wrong map. Maybe just -- Witness, it's -- yeah, it's that map, the blue map. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He can take a look on the screen. It's come up on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Can you see the village of Hrasnica on the map?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Would you draw a circle round it, please. Have you got a pencil?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now, can you see Prozor and Konjic at the bottom on the map? Prozor and Konjic.
