utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: On the map, would you draw in the border between Gornji Vakuf municipality and Prozor and Konjic.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is it evident from this that Hrasnica is not on the border of the Prozor-Konjic municipalities for the Gornji Vakuf municipality? It's not a bordering village, is it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Would it also be correct, then, that Hrasnica does not belong in the report to the villages mentioned as those having been taken control of bordering on the Prozor and Konjic municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the units mentioned and the date confirmed in the document, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in view of the fact that we're dealing with a collective report here and it is for entire period, then following on from that logics, it should record all the more important military operations that the unit took part in or, rather, those military police units took part in that the report refers to. Would that be correct? Do you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the units that I mentioned in the report that would be correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, as far as I understood you, Hrasnica, according to your testimony, was attacked by the military police three times. Would it not be logical, since it was a continuous attack, that this kind of operation would also be mentioned in a report of this nature?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- in my testimony I gave yesterday, I did not say that the military police attacked the village three times. I said the village was attacked three times. On one of those occasions it was the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: But you also said, if I remember correctly, that that village was very important in the military sense. So such an important place would certainly have been recorded, would it not, in a report of this kind? It should have been.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should have been. However, I can refer to the map that General Praljak had up on the board yesterday, and you could see there was a Croatian position on the road just below it. A Bosnian Croat position.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I just asked you about the military police. I wasn't asking you in general. Tell me, please, in your statement you also said that during the negotiations on a cease-fire that a subject of discussion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You referred to General Praljak's map, and I was just consulting it while you were talking. You said that there was a position, an HVO position, under the village, beneath the village at the level of Moscani there were Croatian elements, but opposite them there were ABiH elements, because the village of Hrasnica, on the basis of the map, was lodged between two elements, two BiH elements, and the HVO was opposite the BiH forces. So if there was an offensive on the village, the offensive should have been directed at breaking down the BH lines, ABiH lines. So on the basis of the map you're looking at, with your marker, could you give us the axis of the HVO offensive. Which direction did it take? Where did the HVO forces come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot, Your Honour, because I did not witness it. I just debriefed the patrol of soldiers who did witness it. The actual direction that it came from I cannot say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now, the map with the markings, may it be given an IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Registrar. May we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. That will be Exhibit IC 55, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, during the examination-in-chief -- yes. The witness should sign the map, place his signature and the date on the map, please. I omitted to say that.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And could you just say that the bottom line represents the border between the municipalities of Gornji Vakuf and Prozor and Konjic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I think that today's date is the 18th of October, not the 17th. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, during the examination-in-chief you said that the subject of Hrasnica was a subject discussed a number of times in the negotiations to reach a cease-fire after the attacks; is that right? You remember that? You remember saying that? Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: You also said that during the negotiations the HVO did not deny that that might have been done -- that the attacks might have been carried out by the military police. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in view of the fact that Hrasnica, according to that report of yours, made an impression as an important event, should that subject have been mentioned as a subject of negotiations in one of your reports?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: When you reported on the negotiations, should you have mentioned that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The negotiations were long and time-consuming, and most of the points of the negotiations were passed up our chain of command by our commander, Major Jones or Major Rule, depending on who was in command at the time. Only a brief outline would go into the information summary, and Hrasnica was one of the villages that was visited when we had the -- finally established the proper cease-fire so that the damage could be catalogued.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, can you recall now at least one report of yours mentioning Hrasnica as an item on the agenda at negotiations?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because in all the reports provided to us by the OTP, I have not mentioned to find a single reference to Hrasnica. I have one further question in this connection. In your opinion, does denial imply admission? You already said in response to Mr. Karnavas that failure to deny something could be a tactical move rather than being equivalent to an admission. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And I'd also like to point out that the information summary that you read is the battalion one. It would not be as detailed on my area as the one that I wrote up to the battalion, which would include debriefs from patrols, et cetera, et cetera, and would be anything up to three, four, sometimes five pages long. And they would then take out what they wanted to pass up to our brigade. So you would need to get hold of the Gornji Vakuf daily military information summaries to get more detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, we looked at everything we were provided with. Tell me now, please, I wish to go back to part of your testimony on the first day. It may have been an infelicitous choice of words, but when speaking of the soldiers who chopped off the hand of a handicapped Muslim person - I need not name him because we've already discussed him here - you said that a conflict arose because the Muslims wanted him to be tried in a normal court in Zenica. What do you mean by "normal court"? Was it just a clumsy choice of words or why would the court in Zenica be considered the normal court in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't my opinion, it was their opinion, and they regarded the court in Zenica as the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I now wish to go back to the flag incident. In your statement, you said, and you repeated here, that the flag incident occurred when the Croats raised a flag of the Bosnian Croats and a Muslim policeman fired a shot over the flag as a sign of protest and then he was shot by someone. You confirmed this as being correct today. My question now is: Do you remember having given a statement on the 18th of May and the 22nd of May, 1995, to the OTP of The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I will now read out a part of that statement referring to that event. It reads as follows --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter does not have the exact wording.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: "One day a TV crew filmed a policeman of the Bosnian Croats raising the Croatian flag next to the flag of the Bosnian Muslims. The Muslim policeman fired shots above their heads and started taking down the Croatian flag. Then someone fired a shot at the Muslim policeman as he was taking down the flag." Do you remember this part of your statement?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Would this be the correct description of the event as you remember hearing about it if you didn't see it yourself?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The correct event is the one that's written in the daily military information summary. That -- it did go in that order.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: In your daily infosum it doesn't mention the Bosnian Muslim flag already being flown and the Croatian flag being raised next to it, and there's also no mention of shooting over people's heads.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier, you would need to get the daily information summaries from Gornji Vakuf. It would have been condensed up at Vitez, and they would not have gone into the same amount of detail. They would have removed things and shortened it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: What I read out to you was the statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor. I wish to know whether you abide by this statement or whether what you said then is incorrect. That's what I'd like to know.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was -- there was a Bosnian flag there as well. I never saw the incident, as it says -- as I've said before, I never saw the incident. It was what was reported to us, and it was what our commander dealt with to try to defuse what was a potentially threatening situation to the route.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: But a Bosnian Muslim flag is mentioned here, not a Bosnian flag. But I'm running out of time, so I have another question for you. As far as I was able to understand, as an intelligence officer you received a lot of information from officers or authorised spokespersons of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the ground. Of course, you also received information from the Croatian side, but you did get information from members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We gleaned information from both sides by talking to them on check-points, out on the ground. We also gleaned information of situations further afield by debriefing patrols and convoys as they moved through, and virtually anybody that we could speak to who had seen anything we would speak to and debrief and get them to show us on the map. We kept highly detailed maps of where check-points were, and we needed to know the attitude of the soldiers manning those checkpoints. They were a good combat indicator. If the check-point suddenly -- manning suddenly went up or more check-points appeared, we knew there was a problem in that area. We got information from anywhere and everywhere we could.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: In view of the number of events occurring on the ground and their complexity, and in view of the fact that your main task was to control the roads, if I understood you correctly, is it possible that due to all these circumstances there may have been misinformation? Perhaps you could have been supplied with erroneous information by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina which you were unable to verify properly and completely, thoroughly.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, that is possible. However, both local commanders were present at the talks where our officer commanding Major Rule tried to defuse the situation, and there was no denial from the HVO side that that incident had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, how much time do I have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please. Theoretically, Mr. Coric, you have no time at all because your Defence counsel has had 34 minutes. What do we do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a tricky problem for us, because we have our countdown. We will grant you 10 minutes and no more.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, my name is Valentin Coric. I am an accused. I will unfortunately have to shorten my list of questions, and I will try to put very specific questions relating only to the military police. Everything else I will leave aside. With reference to my report to Bruno Stojic, His Honour Judge Antonetti put quite a few questions, so I will not go into it, but in my opinion, you showed a high degree of knowledge about the organisation of the military police and the army as a whole. Therefore, I will mention one activity, traffic control, and two points, Pavlovica, and Karamustafic. Can you tell me on what road are those two points?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, I can't without a map, but I believe Karamustafic may be by the relay hill, to the south of Gornji Vakuf, but I cannot be specific on that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that those are main roads and that they're significant check-points? Can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I can agree that the -- if that is where Karamustafic is then, yes, it was on the main supply route. Going back to Pavlovica, could that possibly have been the check-point to the north of Gornji Vakuf on the road?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it would assist if the witness would have a map in front of him. It's a bit unfair that he has to give response to these questions without a map.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have time, Your Honours, but I do have a question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that in the first 10 days of January, 1993, these were joint check-points of the military police of the ABiH and the military police of the HVO? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall there were joint check-points, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: I don't have time to show the documents I've prepared, so I'll move on. Did you meet the commander of the military police in Gornji Vakuf on both sides, the HVO and the ABiH? Did you ever meet with them?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall. I don't believe I ever met them, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Does the name Hanafija Prijic, also known as Paraga, mean anything to you? Have you heard of that person?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise the name Paraga, but in why I recognise it I do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Paraga. I'll try and assist you. This person was the commander of the military police at the time. He had about 300 men under his command, and he is connected to the incident when Italian citizens who were involved in humanitarian work were killed. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the incident but I believe it may have occurred just after we left the country. Am I right in saying that Paraga was a Muslim commander and he was at the time of the Gornji Vakuf trouble who was in Bistrica or that area? Did he have a distinctive green beret with two badges on?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the man. I would like to jog your memory. In the town there was a motel which was the headquarters of the Green Berets. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The headquarters of the armija, as I recall, was in a hotel, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Do you remember an explosion that occurred in that hotel?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember there being an explosion at the hotel, and as I recall, and I may be wrong, although there was a significant amount of damage, there was no casualties.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: So no casualties. No one was injured or killed. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall. I can't be specific, but if I remember right, there was an explosion. But as I recall, nobody was injured or killed. But it was one of the general series of incidents that was going on around that time that stoked up what was to occur later on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the sake of brevity, I'll move on. There was another incident when both military police forces were holding that joint check-point. One day, I think it was the 7th -- between the 7th and the 10th of January, all the members of the HVO military police were arrested at those two check-points. Did you hear of that event?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably did at the time, but I don't recall it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened next with regard to those arrests?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't. But which check-point is it you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the two I mentioned before, Pavlovica and Karamustafic. The two most important check-points in the Gornji Vakuf area in the direction towards Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall vaguely that -- that at least one of those check-points was attacked in some way, but I don't remember the ins and outs of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: So the military policemen were arrested by the armed forces of the BH army and taken from the check-point. You don't recall any of the events that ensued in the town of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this goes back to what I said earlier. There was a series of events --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Do you or don't you remember, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember what actually happened to those soldiers, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to assist you. Do you remember that soldiers on both sides were arrested and that an exchange was carried out, so it ended quite peacefully? Do you recall that? And your men participated in that.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a series of exchanges that went on virtually on a daily basis, so I cannot be specific about a particular exchange. Indeed, I was involved in one exchange, but that was civilians. But that one I don't recall. There were exchange nearly every day.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't agree with you there, but I'll ask you another question with Their Honours' indulgence. Did you ever go from the centre of Vakuf town towards the post office and then towards the Ina petrol station and then towards Bugojno? Did you ever pass along that route either in a vehicle or on foot?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that there was fierce fighting throughout the conflict along that line?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I recall, if this is the specific area that I recall correctly, there was even a fight where -- involving a stuffed wild boar where both sides kept seizing it off the other.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very briefly, I wish to jog your memory, Witness, to help you recall several incidents that contributed to the situation. You mentioned the conflict between two villages, a Muslim and a Croat village. Let me remind you that four persons from a Croatian village were cruelly killed with an axe, if you recall. Yesterday, we spoke about a Muslim who had his head chopped off, but what I wish to remind you of is the following: In the report dating from 1992 and presented by my Defence, I -- 1992, and it refers to the period from April to December, it mentions the most significant incidents that had happened in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and do you know that neither more nor less than six are mentioned that relate to Gornji Vakuf? If we compare this to the number of municipalities where the HVO had military police, would you agree, and I hope that when you took up your duties in Gornji Vakuf you were briefed on this, on the 26th there was an armed conflict where people were killed on both sides? Another incident happened on the 4th of August, 1992. That was between those two villages. On the 11th of October, the command of the military police was targeted from a hand-held rocket launcher. All this was in 1992, just before this gentleman arrived to take up his duties. And he arrived in November, as he told us. Then on the 17th of November, 1992, that was when an HVO soldier chopped off the head of a Muslim, and it states clearly here that he was arrested. And all these incidents more or less ended rather well except for the tragedies that occurred. So my next question: When answering Judge Antonetti's question about the reasons why over 20 per cent of the members of the military police were killed in Gornji Vakuf, you were unable to reply. As a professional soldier, could you now enumerate -- I'm just finishing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your time is up. So ask him the last question so that he can answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: My final question is: As the witness was living in Gornji Vakuf in that time period, could he give us the main reasons as to why so many people were killed there? And I did mention the fighting in the town itself. That was my question, my last question.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are going back to when you first built the picture for the question. We were aware that there were frictions between the Muslim and Croatian communities, and we were aware that there had been incidents. However, at the time of our initial deployment, we were not concerned with that. We were just concerned solely with the road and what the warring factions did to each other was, as far as we were concerned, none of our business, so long as we could keep the road open and go where we wanted freely. As to why the casualty rate for the military police was so high, I -- without being told where they were fighting exactly and who they were -- which particular unit they were fighting against, I cannot say. There's many reasons why the casualty rate of particular units may be high. It could be due to poor leadership, lack of fire support.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I have 30 seconds more, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Sir, you did not even know the two main check-points on the road that you're responsible for, Karamustafic and Pavlovica. How then could you know about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric, you need to stop now. You should have worked this out beforehand with your Defence counsel. You should have taken the floor first and let your Defence counsel speak after you. The questions were not of the same nature, I understand, and understand that you're nervous about it, but we have to restrict you time-wise. You were raising your hand, Witness. What did you want to say in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can give Mr. Coric a very quick answer to that. Because we couldn't speak Serbo-Croat and couldn't pronounce the words properly. We gave them code numbers instead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution, do you have any questions for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: In the interests of time, I will not have any additional questions, only to admit the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have a couple of additional questions, Your Honour, based on the questions that were raised. If not, I can just briefly state what those questions are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Mr. Karnavas, there is no question of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... at some point today, I would like to make my record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you want to state for the sake of the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... questions that I wanted to ask. That's what I wanted to state the record for. Basically that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why didn't you ask those questions during the cross-examination time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you for asking that question, Mr. President. Thank you. Because the nature of the questions that I wish to ask arose as a result of questions that were posed by Judge Trechsel. And I think, as I indicated earlier, the common practice has been that counsel on both sides are given opportunities to ask limited questions based on what might have come up through the questioning of the Judges, and that was the reason. It's not something that I forgot or was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But when a Judge puts a question to the witness, the Judge puts a question either because the Prosecution is examining the witness or the Defence. When I put a question and the witness answers, you can still put a question to the witness to clarify a particular point. But some other Defence counsel could be interested in a particular question. They can write it on a piece of paper and give it to you and say, "Be careful. He answered this and that and answered the Judge's question such-and-such a way. Ask this type of question to the witness." It's for you to appreciate the situation. If at the end of each question put by the Bench you have to give the floor to six Defence counsel all in turn to know which additional questions they wish to put, well, then we will never see the end of this. So the best solution is to proceed in the following manner: When you put questions to the witness and when the Bench puts question, you can proceed, but if your other colleagues are interested in this particular issue, it's for them to turn to you and say, for instance, "Mr. Praljak, I'm interested in this. This is what we should do." Because you share the time between you. If you have time left, then you do have time to put the question. But if unfortunately your time has run out, ask your colleague who is putting the question to the witness at that particular time to put the question then to the witness through you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do appreciate all the advice I can get. Sometimes it's after I have already completed my cross-examination that the issues come up, and my colleagues have their own burden to carry, and it's quite a burden, and the last thing they want is for me to be -- to be giving them questions to ask on my behalf. And with all due respect, they're not trained seals. I cannot force them to jump whenever I ask them to jump. In any event, there are just two issues. I can raise them after the witness leaves for the sake of time. I just want to make sure that at least the record is reflected that the questions that were posed, they were posed in such a way that perhaps follow-up questions should have been asked in fairness to the Defence. That's my position, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what were the two questions you wanted to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. One had to do with discipline. Judge Trechsel asked if the gentleman saw any discipline being administered, and he indicated -- I believe his answer was it was brought up at the meetings. The follow-up question would have been, perhaps, did you, sir, being that you were an intelligence officer, did you do anything to verify whether any discipline was occurring, yes or no, as opposed to whether he saw. Also, in light of his previous testimony that he gave, the question would have been: How possible would it have been to have disciplined these rogue elements under the circumstances? Might it have been rather dangerous for a particular low-level commander to try to discipline? I see you're shaking your head, Judge Trechsel. I do think it's relevant. One last -- one last point was where he had indicated -- the gentleman indicated to a question posed by Judge Trechsel, he said that in late January the HVO became more interested in defusing the situation. That answer, that answer seems to -- to indicate that they were not interested prior to that, and of course under -- the follow-up would have been: What makes you believe that they were less interested than before in light of all of your testimony that you had these rogue elements that were not under command and control, not just control but command and control? Everybody was on their own. So those would have been my questions, and I just have them on the record. At least now we're going to try to -- I just want to make sure that we don't -- we don't believe something untouched.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I'm trying to be due diligent as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. We listened to what you had to say, and we have discussed it. We will take note of the questions that you could have asked. I personally consider that the first question was something that the witness already answered, because I think I asked him about how they were disciplined, and the witness said that he didn't know whether there was disciplinary action taken. So he couldn't either confirm or refute it. And I think he answered the question there. Now, as far as your second question, your second point is concerned, in asking the witness this type of question, there could have been a great deal of speculation. But we did take note of your questions and recorded them. But I would like to suggest to both parties that if you feel there are fundamental issues, ask your colleagues to put the question in your name. Otherwise, I'm sure you will understand that every time the Judges ask a question we have to ask the six Defence counsel and then the six accused whether they would like to ask additional questions, and that would keep us here for hours and hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And I would like to make a brief declaration in view of the fact that Counsel Karnavas referred to questions I had put. I would declare that I -- when I put a question always have a slightly bad feeling because I'm quite aware that it is risky to question from the Bench. You cannot object very well to the Bench, and so I feel uneasy and keep, if possible, to a minimum. And I would invite counsel to put follow-up question, and I think that the practice is that we would be on the moment itself prepared to allow that. It's just that we are, as you know and as yourselves have stressed many times, under an extreme time pressure, and now the time has been -- been extended today quite a bit already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel. And I'm just trying to be helpful. And to the extent that I can assist the Trial Chamber, I will continue to do so on every occasion. But I thank you for that invitation, and I will take full advantage of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I am very much aware of the time, but for the record, let me just respond to a couple of things that have been said. My learned colleague Mr. Karnavas is indeed correct that in many instances and many cases the parties are permitted to put questions to the witnesses following questions put by the Bench, and I believe that was actually the practice that we followed in the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura case. With respect to the suggestion that Judge Trechsel just put on the record in terms of follow-up questions, the potential problem, with all due respect, that we see is that, for example, quite often during the course of the direct examination, there will be questions put by the Judges. If at that point in time one of the Defence teams or the accused thinks that a follow-on question to the Judge's question might be in order, we would then have the situation where the direct examination would be even further hampered, thank you, by a series of questions from a number of different parties based on a question from the Bench. And perhaps, and I am hesitant to suggest this, Mr. President and Your Honours, but perhaps one solution to this problem would be to go more towards the model that is more common in the Tribunal in which, to my recollection, was the one that was more the approach that we did take in the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura case. That is the party who is calling the witness and conducting the direct examination is more or less permitted to do that with the bear minimum of questions coming from the Bench. Then we have the cross-examination. And at that point, the Judges would ask the majority of their questions if there were remaining questions that they had or issues that needed further clarification. Now, having said that, I am fully aware that it is the Chamber that controls the proceedings and I am fully aware that there may be instances where it's best to clarify an issue before moving on. But at the same time, if we were to go to a party calling the witness with the bare minimum of interruptions, and I use that word again hesitantly, followed by cross-examination, questions from the Bench, and then any follow-up questions from any of the parties concerning questions from the Bench. That might be a way to solve this -- this dilemma as expeditiously as possible, so that we don't have a situation where everyone is simply jumping up to clarify further questions based on questions coming from the Trial Chamber. And I simply say that as a suggestion with the greatest respect to all of Your Honours and, of course, cognisant of the fact that the Trial Chamber has the authority to control the proceedings. So I simply, again, fully aware of the time, I raise that at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right, but the problem that we're facing with respect to the Hadzihasanovic-Kubura dossier is that we are inundated by thousands of pages of documents. We know that for this witness this is the number of exhibits. So when one of the parties examines the witness on the basis of a document, if we wait to the end in a few days' time to go back to the document, then we have to take up the document again, whereas we have the document in front of us now. So it would be better to wait to the end if we don't have the documents. But since we do have the documents, orders, et cetera, then we have to intervene straight away, because afterwards it's too late and we can't ask the question two days later. So that is a real problem, and it's here because we have thousands of pages that everybody is examining, and sometimes we have to go straight to the heart of the matter. But as a general rule, when the Judge asks a question, the question takes into account all the elements, and the answer given to the Judge's question, in theory, should not raise -- give rise to additional questions, to redirect, because everything has already been said. So if we're asking the witness -- if we ask the witness can you tell us whether in such-and-such a village there was a check-point or not, if the Judge asks that type of question, the witness answers, no, there wasn't, for example, and unless the Defence has a document to prove the contrary, there's no need to take up the matter again and ask the question again unless the witness was wrong. Then you can produce a document to show that, that the witness was either lying or was wrong or whatever. But the questions are put in such a way that they do not require additional questions. Having said that, we'd like to thank you, Witness, for having come to testify and make your contribution. I'm afraid we kept you longer than initially expected. You've been here for three days now. We thank you for that. I'm going to ask Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom. And I'm going to ask the registrar to lower the blinds because we're going to put in place protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're also going to take the break straight away. As far as admission of exhibits is concerned, we'll leave that to another time. It's quarter past 5.00 or 20 past 5.00. Let's say 20 past 5.00. So we reconvene in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. We'll go into private session, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: At the time when you were asked the questions by the investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor, you answered the questions truthfully?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: You did this voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: And you remember the statement being read back to you at the end of the interview with the investigator in your own language?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: And you remember signing that statement?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Could you take a look at the statements that are to your left-hand side -- sorry, right-hand side. Can you take --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am illiterate. I do not know how to read or write. I think it says so in my statement, that I declared that. I cannot read. I did not go to school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I will resolve that difficulty. Sir, do you remember that an investigator, when he asked you to sign his document, through an interpreter, read back the statement to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. And the text that was read back to you in your own language, did it correspond to the questions that the investigator asked you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. There were some small changes. At my request he put that right, and everything was in order then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means that the document that you signed corresponds to what you told the investigator.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Finally, Witness, do you stand by the contents of that document as being true to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything I said in the statement I stand by. It is 100 per cent correct and true.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: On page 4 of the English version of the statement and also the B/C/S version of this statement, you talk about you and your nephew being in a column. Do you remember that part of your statement?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Who else was in the column with you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you all the names, but I know most of the names of the people who were there, and if need be, I can give you a few of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Be careful not to name names, name his relatives' names or things like that, because we're going to have to waste time redacting the transcript if he does.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Witness, if I can turn to an exhibit numbered 1326. On page 4 of the English version of that particular document is a list of names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Usher, would you help the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Noting, Witness, what you have said about your reading ability, it is probably easier if I read the list of names to you, but what I would like you to do is after each name, could you answer yes or no as to whether that person was in the column with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. We'll move into private session in case there are any names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 19th day of October, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.04 p.m.,
